1177.title: Quoting and changing
1177.hook: he kept adding to the Essays in the margins until he died
1177.howItsDone: Montaigne says in the essay Of vanity that he adds to his book but does not correct it, and in Of books that he borrows other writers' words to say what he cannot say as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a Catholic doubter: Montaigne asked what do I know? and stayed in his church. Your line was faith and doubt.

Open a secondhand book and sometimes there's a stranger in it: pencil in the margins, a word underlined, a question mark, a date, a small argument with the author. Tradition says Montaigne did something like that to his own book. Once the Essays were printed and out in the world, he kept adding to them: new sentences, new quotations, second thoughts that didn't erase the first ones. Today, a book that never quite stopped being written, and the man who said why.
screen: `PENCIL IN THE MARGINS.` → `HIS OWN PRINTED BOOK.` → `SECOND THOUGHTS, FIRST ONES KEPT.`

segments.voice: First, his rule. In the essay Of vanity, Montaigne says it plainly: I add, but I don't correct. Once the book had gone out, he felt it belonged partly to its readers. And he wasn't sure his later self was wiser than his earlier one. Myself now and myself a while ago, he says, are indeed two. So the old self keeps its say, and the new self adds a note beside it. Second, the quoting. His pages are full of other people's words, many of them in Latin. In the essay Of books he explains: he makes others say what he can't say so well himself. Third, his trick. Sometimes, he admits, he leaves the author's name off on purpose. That way a critic who sneers at the line, thinking it's his, ends up flicking Plutarch on the nose, or burning his fingers insulting Seneca. Fourth, what this makes the book. Not a monument but a conversation: his voice and the old voices, his younger thoughts and his older ones, all left standing on the same page. Your life has old pages too: a letter, a journal, an opinion you once held loudly. You don't have to tear them out. You can write beside them.

1178.title: Himself as subject
1178.hook: I am myself the matter of my book, he tells the reader
1178.howItsDone: Montaigne's Essays open with a short note to the reader saying the book was written for his family and friends, and that he himself is its subject, painted plainly, faults and all.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was quoting and changing: Montaigne added to his book but didn't correct it. Your line was keep adding.

The first page of Montaigne's book doesn't invite you in. It tells you to stop reading. Before the first essay comes a short note headed To the reader. It's a book of good faith, he says, written for his family and friends, so that after they lose him, they can find some trace of him again. Then the last lines: I am myself the matter of my book. You'd be unreasonable, reader, to spend your free time on a subject so slight and so vain. So, farewell.
screen: `A NOTE: TO THE READER.` → `FOR FAMILY AND FRIENDS.` → `SO, FAREWELL.`

segments.voice: First, who it was for. He had no thought of serving the reader, he says, or of his own glory. He wrote so the people who knew him could keep something of him after he died. Second, how he wanted to be seen. If he'd wanted the world's favor, he'd have dressed himself up. Instead he wants to be seen in his simple, natural, ordinary way, without strain or artifice, because it's himself he's painting. His faults will be there to read. Third, the subject. I am myself the matter of my book. Not kings, not wars, not the nature of the universe, though he touches all of those: one ordinary man, looked at honestly from the inside. Then the joke: why waste your time on that? Farewell. Of course, the reader doesn't leave. Fourth, what writing himself did to him. In a later essay he turns it around: I have no more made my book than my book has made me. Painting himself for others, he says, he painted his inside in clearer colors than before. The writing changed the writer. You don't need to publish anything for that. One honest paragraph about yourself, even one nobody reads, can show you to yourself in clearer colors.

1179.title: The essay as a practice
1179.hook: an essay is a trying-out, and so is a life
1179.howItsDone: Readers often take Montaigne's own play on the word essais, trials or attempts, as a way of living: trying out thoughts and habits as experiments rather than settling everything at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was himself as subject: I am myself the matter of my book. Your line was myself the matter.

A river with no bridge. You want to cross, but you can't see the bottom. So you push a long stick in, a little way out from the bank. Shallow. A little farther. Still fine. Farther, and the stick disappears and keeps going. You step back onto the bank. Nobody calls that failure; you found out where the bottom was. Montaigne uses almost that exact picture for how he puts his judgment to work. Today, the name he gave the whole thing.
screen: `A RIVER WITH NO BRIDGE.` → `PUSH A STICK IN.` → `TOO DEEP: BACK TO THE BANK.`

segments.voice: First, the ford. In an early essay, Montaigne says judgment is a tool for every subject, and he tries it on all of them, even ones he doesn't understand. He sounds the ford from far off. If it's too deep for his height, he stays on the bank. And knowing he can't cross is itself something his judgment learned. Second, the word. He called his book Essais, and in the essay Of repentance he tells us what he means, roughly: if my mind could find firm footing, I wouldn't be essaying myself, trying myself out; I'd be making up my mind. But it's always in apprenticeship and on trial. So the essays aren't verdicts. They're tests, with himself as the material. Third, what that frees him to do. A trial can fail and still teach. He can try out an opinion on Monday and its opposite on Thursday, and both go in the book. He isn't building a system; he's checking the depth, stick in hand. Fourth, the life. Read that way, an essay is less a school assignment and more a practice. Try a thought, a habit, a kinder answer to someone who annoys you. Too deep: back to the bank, no shame. If it holds, take another step. Big, frozen decisions become small experiments you can actually begin.

1180.title: A virtue gripped too hard
1180.hook: Montaigne distrusts extremes, even in virtue
1180.carry: even a virtue, gripped too hard, becomes a fault
1180.howItsDone: In the essay Of moderation, Montaigne argues that even good things, virtue included, can be spoiled by being grasped too violently, and he appeals to Saint Paul's call to think soberly.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the essay as a practice: Montaigne's essays are trials, a stick pushed into the river. Your line was a trying-out.

A friend starts running. Good. Then it's every morning, then twice a day, then the knees give out and the running stops completely. Another friend decides to be honest, really honest, and within a week has told three people exactly what's wrong with their haircuts, their marriages and their cooking. Both goals were good. Something went wrong anyway. Montaigne has an essay about exactly this, and it says something unexpected: you can hold even a virtue too tightly.
screen: `RUNNING, THEN TOO MUCH RUNNING.` → `HONEST, THEN TOO HONEST.` → `A VIRTUE HELD TOO TIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: First, the image. In the essay Of moderation, Montaigne says it's as if our touch were infectious. We take hold of things that are good in themselves and spoil them by how we handle them. Second, the claim. We can grip virtue so hard, he says, with such violent desire, that it turns into a fault. He knows the objection: some say there can't be too much virtue, because once it's excessive it isn't virtue anymore. Montaigne calls that playing with words. In real life, people do overdo good things. Third, his witness. He points to a line of Saint Paul, from the letter to the Romans. In the King James Bible it reads: "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly." Montaigne hears in it a call to be wise with measure, not to push even wisdom past its proper size. Fourth, what this asks. Not to care less. He isn't asking anyone to be lukewarm about being kind or honest or healthy. He's asking for a grip that doesn't crush what it holds: honesty that still leaves the other person standing, discipline that still leaves the knees working, devotion that still leaves room for dinner with friends.

1181.title: The art of conversation
1181.hook: he loved a good, sharp conversation and hated flattery (Essays 3.8)
1181.howItsDone: In the essay Of the art of conversing, Montaigne describes welcoming contradiction as a teacher and disliking talk where everyone only agrees; readers often take it as a guide to disagreeing well.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was not too much: we can grip even a virtue so hard it turns into a fault. Your line was not too much.

Somebody at the table says something you think is wrong. A few moves are available. Nod and change the subject. Agree out loud and disagree in the car on the way home. Or say, wait, I don't think that's right, and see what happens. Montaigne knew which one he wanted, from himself and from whoever was talking with him. He wrote a whole essay about talking, and in it he says he'd rather be contradicted than flattered.
screen: `SOMEONE SAYS SOMETHING WRONG.` → `NOD, OR SAY IT?` → `CONTRADICT ME, PLEASE.`

segments.voice: First, how much he prized it. In the essay Of the art of conversing, Montaigne calls conversation the most fruitful and natural exercise of our minds. He finds it sweeter than any other act of life, so much that he'd sooner give up his sight than his hearing or his speech. Second, what he wanted from it. Not agreement. When someone opposes him, he says, it wakes his attention, not his anger. He moves toward the person who contradicts him, because that person is teaching him. Truth is welcome from any hand, and he means to give it a cheerful welcome, even when it beats him. Third, what he couldn't stand. Talk where everyone defers and applauds bores him; he calls that kind of company soft. He wants a friendship strong enough to enjoy sharpness and vigor in the way people talk. Flattery wastes the whole point: if the other person only agrees, nothing gets tested. Fourth, the hard part. Much of the essay is about how talk goes wrong: people get heated, stubborn, more attached to winning than to finding out. His art isn't about being clever. It's about caring more for the truth than for your own side of the table. Sometimes that's one sentence: I see it differently, and here's why. Then listening to the answer.

1182.title: Sleep and food
1182.hook: he wrote frankly about his habits of eating and sleeping (Essays 3.13)
1182.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take the eating and sleeping passages of Of experience as permission to treat daily needs as part of a good life rather than a distraction from it; some use them as a cue to eat one meal a day without hurry.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the art of conversation: Montaigne liked his talk sharp and had no use for flattery. Your line was honest talk.

A philosopher at dinner bites his own tongue. Sometimes his fingers. He eats too fast, he admits. He loves sauces, though his father hated them. Salads and fruit, not much, except melons. He can manage without a tablecloth, but a clean napkin he really wants. This isn't a servant's gossip. It's Montaigne, writing about himself in Of experience, the closing essay of his book. Why would a serious writer put his napkins next to his thoughts on death and God?
screen: `HE BITES HIS OWN TONGUE.` → `SAUCES, MELONS, A CLEAN NAPKIN.` → `WHY PUT THIS IN A BOOK?`

segments.voice: First, the plain facts, given plainly. Sleep, he says, has taken up a large part of his life. He likes his bed hard, and he likes to sleep alone, well covered. He eats greedily and in a hurry. He knows which foods agree with him and which habits he'd do better to break. He isn't confessing. He's reporting, the way you'd describe the weather. Second, the reason. Nature, Montaigne says, has been like a mother here. The things we have to do to stay alive, she made pleasant too, and she calls us to them not only through reason but through appetite. Eating and sleeping aren't a tax paid before the real life starts. They're part of the gift. Third, his quarrel. Some people count an act as less worthy because it's necessary, as if eating and sleeping were beneath a serious mind. Montaigne won't have it. Nobody, he says, will get it out of his head that pleasure and necessity make a very fitting marriage. He wants the mind to keep the body company at the table, not sit apart from it, sniffing. Fourth, an ordinary day. A warm bowl of something when you're cold. The first sip of water when you're thirsty. Lying down at night and feeling the weight leave your feet. Montaigne would count every one, not as the reward for a day well spent, but as the day itself, being lived. A man who wrote down so many doubts still thought a good night's sleep belonged in the book.

segments.voice: Enjoy one ordinary pleasure, on purpose: if there's a drink nearby, take a slow sip and actually taste it, and if not, notice the pleasure already here, the chair holding you up, warm hands, a full breath going all the way down. 1183.title: What to keep from Montaigne
1183.hook: curiosity, doubt, gentleness, laughter at ourselves
1183.howItsDone: Readers who spend time with Montaigne often come away keeping one habit rather than a doctrine, such as asking 'what do I know?' before judging, or laughing at their own self-importance.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sleep and food: Montaigne says nature made our needs pleasant on purpose. Your line was ordinary pleasures.

Moving day. The truck comes at nine, the boxes are full, and there's one small bag left for the things you won't let the movers touch. Not much fits, so you choose. Montaigne's book is a big, rambling house of a book, with a room for nearly everything, and tomorrow this path closes the door on it. Today is the small bag. Four things seem worth carrying out: curiosity, doubt, gentleness, and laughter at ourselves.
screen: `ONE SMALL BAG.` → `A BIG, RAMBLING BOOK.` → `FOUR THINGS TO CARRY OUT.`

segments.voice: First, curiosity. Montaigne wanted to know how other people lived. He loved travel for the new and the different, and he turned the same curiosity on himself: his moods, his habits, his own changing mind. Nothing was too small to look at. Second, doubt. He took a question as a kind of motto: what do I know? Not despair. A brake. It kept him from being too sure, especially when being sure meant condemning someone. A man who doubts his own judgment is slower to burn a neighbor for a witch. Third, gentleness. He hated cruelty, and said so, even cruelty to animals. When he played with his cat, he wondered whether she was playing with him. A gentle mind leaves room for the other creature's point of view. Fourth, laughter at ourselves. On the highest throne in the world, he says, we still sit on our own bottom. He didn't laugh at other people's faith or pain, only at the human habit of taking ourselves too seriously, starting with his own. The four hold each other up. Curiosity without doubt turns into collecting opinions to win arguments. Doubt without gentleness turns cold. Gentleness without laughter gets heavy. Laughter without curiosity is just mockery. At the very end of his book, Montaigne asks not for a severe wisdom, but for a cheerful and sociable one. If only one thing fits in the bag, today's line picks curiosity, because it keeps the other three moving.
screen: `CURIOSITY: NOTHING TOO SMALL.` · `DOUBT: WHAT DO I KNOW?` · `GENTLENESS: ROOM FOR THE CAT.` · `LAUGHTER: STARTING WITH HIMSELF.` · then, large: `A CHEERFUL AND SOCIABLE WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Say the four quietly, curiosity, doubt, gentleness, laughter, and notice which one tugs at you, maybe because you have it, maybe because you don't. Then let a real moment from this week come to mind, a hard conversation, a quick judgment, a bad mood, and hold that quality up to it like a lamp, just looking at what it would have changed.
